To braid means to take three or more separate strands and weave them over and under each other — in a specific, repeating crossing pattern — until they form a single, unified structure.

The key word is crossing. You are not just twisting strands together. You are moving each strand diagonally across the others, one at a time, in a rhythmic over-under sequence. The result is a structure with a distinctive diagonal, herringbone-like pattern running along its length.
The minimum requirement: three strands

This is important. You cannot truly braid with only two strands — that is just twisting. Braiding requires at least three strands, because the logic of a braid depends on one strand always having two others to cross between.
How it actually works (the logic)

Imagine three strands — call them Left, Middle, and Right — hanging side by side.

  • You take the Left strand and cross it over the Middle. Now it becomes the new Middle.
  • Then you take the Right strand and cross it over the (new) Middle. Now it becomes the new Middle.
  • You keep repeating this — left over middle, right over middle, left over middle — and a braid grows downward.

Every strand takes turns being the one that crosses. No strand stays in one place permanently. The continuous, orderly crossing is what creates the tight, interlocked pattern.
What braiding achieves

Braiding is not just decorative. It serves real purposes:

  • Strength — Braided rope or cable is significantly stronger than a single thick strand of the same material, because the load is distributed across multiple crossing strands.
  • Flexibility — A braid bends more easily than a solid rod of the same thickness.
  • Neatness — Loose strands (especially hair) are gathered into a compact, controlled shape that holds together without glue or binding.
Where you encounter this verb
The verb is used across a surprisingly wide range of contexts:
Hair

"She braids her hair every night before bed."
This is the most familiar use. Sections of hair are separated and crossed over each other repeatedly. The resulting structure stays together because the strands grip each other through friction and tension.
Bread dough

"The baker braided the dough into a loaf before baking."
Long ropes of dough are woven together. When baked, the loaf holds its braided shape. Challah bread is a famous example.
Rope, cord, and wire

"Workers braided thick steel cables for the suspension bridge."
Industrial rope is almost always braided rather than twisted, for the strength reasons mentioned above. Paracord, friendship bracelets, and decorative trim on clothing are all made by braiding.
Leather and fabric

"He braided strips of leather to make a belt."
Thin strips of material are braided into straps, handles, or decorative edging.
Rugs

"She braided old fabric scraps into a rug."
Strips of cloth are braided into long ropes, which are then coiled and sewn flat to form a rug.
The figurative use

Because braiding is about taking separate things and weaving them into something unified, English uses it figuratively to describe how ideas, stories, or elements are woven together.

"The novel braids three different storylines across four decades."
"The speech braided personal memoir with political argument."

Here, "braid" means: the elements are not simply placed side by side — they are interlocked and interwoven so that each passes through and influences the others, the way strands in a physical braid do. The image carries the idea of interdependence and unified complexity.
Braiding vs. similar actions — a clear distinction

It helps to know where braiding ends and other things begin:

  • Twisting — Only two strands spiraling around each other. No crossing pattern. Much weaker than a braid.
  • Weaving — Strands cross at right angles (horizontal and vertical), typically on a loom. The result is a flat fabric. Braiding involves diagonal crossing and produces a rope-like or flat-tape structure.
  • Knotting — Strands are looped and pulled through each other to create fixed points. Braiding is continuous and flowing, not knotted.
  • Plaiting — This word means exactly the same thing as braiding. The two are interchangeable. (British English tends to prefer plait; American English tends to prefer braid.)
Tightness and style

A braid can be done tightly (strands pulled firmly together, creating a dense, compact structure) or loosely (strands barely crossing, creating an airy, relaxed look). The same crossing technique applies either way; only the tension differs.

More complex braids involve more strands — four, five, six, or more — with more elaborate crossing sequences. A French braid, for instance, is a three-strand braid where new hair is added into each strand as you go, so the braid gradually incorporates all the hair from the scalp rather than just a portion. The verb "to braid" covers all of these variations.
In summary

To braid is to weave three or more strands over and under each other in a continuous, repeating crossing pattern, producing a single unified structure that is stronger, neater, or more complex than its individual strands. The action applies equally to hair, rope, dough, leather, wire, and — figuratively — to narratives, themes, and ideas.
